questions.qtext:
Consider the Context-Free Grammar (CFG) $G=(V, \Sigma, P, S)$, where $S$ is the start symbol, $\Sigma=\{a, b\}$ is the set of terminal symbols, $V=\{S, B\}$ is the set of non-terminals, and the set of production rules $P$ is defined by:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& S \longrightarrow S B \mid a a \\
& B \longrightarrow b S B b \mid a b
\end{aligned}
$$
Let $|w|_{a}$ denote the number of occurrences of the terminal symbol $a$ in a string $w$, and let $|w|_{b}$ denote the number of occurrences of the terminal symbol $b$ in $w$.
Which of the following equations correctly describes the relationship between the number of $a$ 's and $b$ 's for all terminal strings $w \in L(G)$ ?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 0)
Take any one string generated by grammar $G$:

$S \Rightarrow SB \Rightarrow aaB \Rightarrow aabSBb \Rightarrow aabaaBb \Rightarrow aabaaabb$

In string $w = aabaaabb$, $ | w|_a = 5$ and $|w|_b = 3$

This eliminates options $B$, $C$, $D$.

So, A is correct answer.

questions.qtext:
Consider the Context-Free Grammar $G:$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& S \longrightarrow A S A \mid a B \\
& A \longrightarrow B \mid S \\
& B \longrightarrow b \mid \epsilon
\end{aligned}
$$
Which of the following strings is/are generated by this grammar ?
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Answer: $\boxed{\text{A, B, C}}$

$A)$ $bba$ is in $\text{L(G)}$:

$B)$ $ab$ is in $\text{L(G)}$:

$S \Rightarrow aB \Rightarrow ab$

$C)$ $ba$ is in $\text{L(G)}$:

$S \Rightarrow ASA \Rightarrow BSA \Rightarrow bSA \Rightarrow baBA \Rightarrow baA \Rightarrow baB \Rightarrow ba$

$D)$ $bb$ is not in $\text{L(G)}$ because there will be at least one 'a' in the strings generated by grammar because you eventually have to apply second $S$ production (i.e. $S \to aB$) and it contains 'a'.

questions.qtext:
Consider the Grammar $G:$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& S \longrightarrow \epsilon \mid a T \mid b T \\
& T \longrightarrow a S \mid b S
\end{aligned}
$$
Which of the following statements is/are incorrect ?

options.text: Every terminal string $w \in L(G)$ has an even length.
The string $a a b b$ can be derived and is accepted by $G$.
The string $b a b b$ cannot be derived and is not accepted by $G$.
There exists at least one string of even length that does not belong to $L(G)$.

questions.solution:
Answer: C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Let's first simplify the grammar. Apply $T$ productions in $aT$ and $bT$:

$S \longrightarrow \epsilon \mid aaS \mid abS \mid baS \mid bbS $

Langauge of grammar is set of all even length strings.

Regular expression: ${(aa + ab + ba + bb)}^*$

  1. Every terminal string $w \in L(G)$ has an even length. $\color{blue}\boxed{{\text{Correct}}}$
  2. The string $a a b b$ can be derived and is accepted by $G$. $\color{blue}\boxed{{\text{Correct}}}$
    True. $aabb$ has even length. Therefore, $aabb \in L(G)$
  3. The string $b a b b$ cannot be derived and is not accepted by $G$. $\color{red}\boxed{{\text{Incorrect}}}$
    No, $babb$ has even length and therefore, $babb\in L(G)$
  4. There exists at least one string of even length that does not belong to $L(G)$. $\color{red}\boxed{{\text{Incorrect}}}$
    False because every even length string belongs to $L(G)$.
Answer: $\boxed{\text{C, D}}$

questions.qtext: The following grammar is ambiguous: $$\begin{aligned}&S\to AB\\&A\to aA\mid a\\&B\to aB\mid a\end{aligned}$$ Which of the following pairs of derivations correctly prove that the grammar is ambiguous?

options.text:
$S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow aAB\Rightarrow aaB\Rightarrow aaa$
$S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow Aa\Rightarrow aAa\Rightarrow aaa$

$S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow aAB\Rightarrow aaB\Rightarrow aaa$
$S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow aB\Rightarrow aaB\Rightarrow aaa$

$S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow Aa\Rightarrow aAa\Rightarrow aaa$
$S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow AaB\Rightarrow Aaa\Rightarrow aaa$

$S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow aAB\Rightarrow aaB\Rightarrow aaa$
$S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow aB\Rightarrow aa$

questions.solution:
Answer: B, C, A

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Answer: $\boxed{\text{B, C}}$

To prove ambiguity of a CFG grammar $\mathrm{G}$, we must show at least two different leftmost derivations of a same string, or show at least two different rightmost derivations of a same string, or show at least two different parse trees of a same string.

Option A :
Mix of left/rightmost derivations.

Option B :
Two different leftmost derivations of $\mathrm{aaa}$

Option C :
Two different rightmost derivations of $\mathrm{aaa}$

Option D :
Two different strings, not two LMD or two RMD derivations of same string
